claim: Current SARS-CoV-2 vaccines are losing efficacy against emerging variants.
source: Current SARS-CoV-2 vaccines are losing efficacy against emerging variants and may not protect against future novel coronavirus outbreaks, emphasizing the need for more broadly protective vaccines.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a motivation for the study, drawing on established knowledge about vaccine performance against variants.

claim: There is an 11- to 123-fold increase in antibodies binding to SARS-CoV and MERS-CoV in COVID-19 convalescent sera compared to pre-pandemic healthy donors.
source: We found an 11- to 123-fold increase in antibodies binding to SARS-CoV and MERS-CoV as well as a 2- to 4-fold difference in antibodies binding to seasonal hCoVs in COVID-19 convalescent sera compared to pre-pandemic healthy donors, with the S2 subdomain of the S protein being the main target for cross-reactivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the Luminex assay comparing COVID-19 patient sera to healthy donor sera.

claim: There is a 2- to 4-fold difference in antibodies binding to seasonal hCoVs in COVID-19 convalescent sera compared to pre-pandemic healthy donors.
source: We found an 11- to 123-fold increase in antibodies binding to SARS-CoV and MERS-CoV as well as a 2- to 4-fold difference in antibodies binding to seasonal hCoVs in COVID-19 convalescent sera compared to pre-pandemic healthy donors, with the S2 subdomain of the S protein being the main target for cross-reactivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the Luminex assay comparing COVID-19 patient sera to healthy donor sera.

claim: The S2 subdomain of the S protein is the main target for cross-reactivity.
source: We found an 11- to 123-fold increase in antibodies binding to SARS-CoV and MERS-CoV as well as a 2- to 4-fold difference in antibodies binding to seasonal hCoVs in COVID-19 convalescent sera compared to pre-pandemic healthy donors, with the S2 subdomain of the S protein being the main target for cross-reactivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by depletion experiments showing greater reduction of cross-reactive antibodies after S2 subdomain depletion compared to S1 subdomain depletion.

claim: Cross-reactive antibodies to all hCoV S proteins are detected after SARS-CoV-2 vaccination in macaques.
source: In addition, we detected cross-reactive antibodies to all hCoV S proteins after SARS-CoV-2 vaccination in macaques and humans, with higher responses for hCoV more closely related to SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from vaccinated cynomolgus macaques showing increased antibody binding to all hCoV S proteins.

claim: Cross-reactive antibodies to all hCoV S proteins are detected after SARS-CoV-2 vaccination in humans.
source: In addition, we detected cross-reactive antibodies to all hCoV S proteins after SARS-CoV-2 vaccination in macaques and humans, with higher responses for hCoV more closely related to SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from vaccinated SARS-CoV-2-naïve individuals showing increased antibody binding to hCoV S proteins.

claim: Higher cross-reactive responses are observed for hCoV more closely related to SARS-CoV-2.
source: In addition, we detected cross-reactive antibodies to all hCoV S proteins after SARS-CoV-2 vaccination in macaques and humans, with higher responses for hCoV more closely related to SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing stronger responses to SARS-CoV and MERS-CoV compared to seasonal coronaviruses, and correlation with sequence identity.

claim: These findings support the feasibility of development of a pan-coronavirus vaccine.
source: These findings support the feasibility of and provide guidance for development of a pan-coronavirus vaccine.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings showing cross-reactive antibody responses.

claim: COVID-19 vaccines show reduced efficacy against emerging SARS-CoV-2 variants.
source: However, these vaccines show reduced efficacy against emerging SARS-CoV-2 variants and vaccine breakthrough infections are frequently reported (Madhi et al., 2021; Lopez Bernal et al., 2021; Kustin et al., 2021; Hacisuleyman et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Vaccine breakthrough infections are frequently reported.
source: However, these vaccines show reduced efficacy against emerging SARS-CoV-2 variants and vaccine breakthrough infections are frequently reported (Madhi et al., 2021; Lopez Bernal et al., 2021; Kustin et al., 2021; Hacisuleyman et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 is the fifth coronavirus to infect humans discovered in less than two decades.
source: New coronaviruses that infect humans (hCoVs) emerge frequently, and SARS-CoV-2 is the fifth to be discovered in less than two decades, bringing the total up to seven (Kahn and McIntosh, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: There are seven coronaviruses that infect humans in total.
source: New coronaviruses that infect humans (hCoVs) emerge frequently, and SARS-CoV-2 is the fifth to be discovered in less than two decades, bringing the total up to seven (Kahn and McIntosh, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Seasonal coronaviruses account for approximately 5–30% of common colds during the winter season.
source: These include the seasonal betacoronaviruses hCoV-OC43 and hCoV-HKU1 as well as alphacoronaviruses hCoV-NL63 and hCoV-229E, which usually cause mild respiratory symptoms and account for approximately 5–30% of common colds during the winter season (Zhu et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: SARS-CoV and MERS-CoV led to epidemics in 2003 and 2013–2015, respectively.
source: In contrast, severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS)-CoV and Middle Eastern Respiratory Syndrome (MERS)-CoV are far more pathogenic and led to epidemics in 2003 and 2013–2015, respectively (da Costa et al., 2020; de Wit et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The S protein of SARS-CoV-2 shows approximately 75% amino acid sequence identity to the S protein of SARS-CoV.
source: The S protein of SARS-CoV-2 is most closely related to the S protein of SARS-CoV (~75% amino acid sequence identity), shows less similarity to MERS-CoV S protein (~50% identity), and is more distinct from the S proteins of the seasonal hCoVs (~25–30% identity) (Lu et al., 2020; Barnes et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The S protein of SARS-CoV-2 shows approximately 50% amino acid sequence identity to MERS-CoV S protein.
source: The S protein of SARS-CoV-2 is most closely related to the S protein of SARS-CoV (~75% amino acid sequence identity), shows less similarity to MERS-CoV S protein (~50% identity), and is more distinct from the S proteins of the seasonal hCoVs (~25–30% identity) (Lu et al., 2020; Barnes et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The S protein of SARS-CoV-2 shows approximately 25–30% amino acid sequence identity to the S proteins of seasonal hCoVs.
source: The S protein of SARS-CoV-2 is most closely related to the S protein of SARS-CoV (~75% amino acid sequence identity), shows less similarity to MERS-CoV S protein (~50% identity), and is more distinct from the S proteins of the seasonal hCoVs (~25–30% identity) (Lu et al., 2020; Barnes et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Several studies observed cross-reactivity of COVID-19 sera against other hCoVs.
source: Although this sequence identity is considered low from the perspective of eliciting cross-reactive antibodies by vaccination, several studies observed cross-reactivity of COVID-19 sera against other hCoVs (Westerhuis et al., 2020; Dugas et al., 2021; Ng et al., 2020; Aydillo et al., 2021; Song et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: Broader hCoV monoclonal antibodies have been isolated and engineered.
source: In addition, the isolation and engineering of broader hCoV monoclonal antibodies have been reported (Wec et al., 2020; Rappazzo et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Sera from convalescent COVID-19 patients showed 990-fold higher antibody levels to SARS-CoV-2 S protein compared to pre-pandemic healthy donor sera.
source: Sera from convalescent COVID-19 patients showed 990-fold higher antibody levels to SARS-CoV-2 S protein compared to pre-pandemic healthy donor sera (median 3.8 log10 vs. 0.8 log10 median fluorescent intensity [MFI], p<0.0001) (Figure 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the Luminex assay shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Hospitalized COVID-19 patients had fourfold higher antibody levels compared to nonhospitalized patients.
source: When subdividing the convalescent patients based on admission status, fourfold higher antibody levels were observed for hospitalized patients compared to nonhospitalized patients (median 4.1 log10 vs. 3.5 log10 MFI, p<0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the Luminex assay comparing hospitalized and nonhospitalized patients.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 neutralization capacity was significantly higher (fivefold) in hospitalized patients.
source: SARS-CoV-2 neutralization capacity was also significantly higher (fivefold) in hospitalized patients (3.6 log10 vs. 2.9 log10 MFI, p<0.0001), and antibody levels and neutralization capacity were strongly correlated in all patients (Spearman's r = 0.735, p<0.0001) (Figure 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the neutralization assay shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Antibody levels and neutralization capacity were strongly correlated in all patients (Spearman's r = 0.735, p<0.0001).
source: SARS-CoV-2 neutralization capacity was also significantly higher (fivefold) in hospitalized patients (3.6 log10 vs. 2.9 log10 MFI, p<0.0001), and antibody levels and neutralization capacity were strongly correlated in all patients (Spearman's r = 0.735, p<0.0001) (Figure 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: An eightfold higher antibody response to the SARS-CoV-2 S protein was observed in the oldest age group of COVID-19 patients (age >60) compared to the youngest age group (age <35).
source: An eightfold higher antibody response to the SARS-CoV-2 S protein was observed in the oldest age group of COVID-19 patients (age >60) compared to the youngest age group (age <35) (4.1 log10 vs. 3.2 log10 MFI, p<0.001), which is in line with age being a risk factor for severe COVID-19 (Figure 1a; Williamson et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the Luminex assay shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Age is a risk factor for severe COVID-19.
source: An eightfold higher antibody response to the SARS-CoV-2 S protein was observed in the oldest age group of COVID-19 patients (age >60) compared to the youngest age group (age <35) (4.1 log10 vs. 3.2 log10 MFI, p<0.001), which is in line with age being a risk factor for severe COVID-19 (Figure 1a; Williamson et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: No difference in antibody levels was observed between sex.
source: No difference in antibody levels was observed between sex (3.8 log10 vs. 3.9 log10 MFI, p=0.71).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the Luminex assay.

claim: Significantly higher levels of antibodies binding to all hCoV S proteins were found in convalescent COVID-19 sera compared to pre-pandemic healthy donor sera.
source: We found significantly higher levels of antibodies binding to all hCoV S proteins in convalescent COVID-19 sera compared to pre-pandemic healthy donor sera, with the largest difference for SARS-CoV and MERS-CoV S protein (123- and 11-fold difference between medians, respectively, p<0.0001 for both proteins) (Figure 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the Luminex assay shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The largest difference in antibody binding was for SARS-CoV and MERS-CoV S protein (123- and 11-fold difference between medians, respectively).
source: We found significantly higher levels of antibodies binding to all hCoV S proteins in convalescent COVID-19 sera compared to pre-pandemic healthy donor sera, with the largest difference for SARS-CoV and MERS-CoV S protein (123- and 11-fold difference between medians, respectively, p<0.0001 for both proteins) (Figure 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the Luminex assay shown in Figure 2a.

claim: For the circulating seasonal hCoVs, a two- to fourfold difference in median levels of antibodies binding to the S proteins was observed.
source: For the circulating seasonal hCoVs, a two- to fourfold difference in median levels of antibodies binding to the S proteins was observed; hCoV-OC43 (4.2-fold, p<0.0001), hCoV-HKU1 (4.3-fold, p<0.0001), hCoV-229E (3.8-fold, p<0.0001), and hCoV-NL63 (1.8-fold, p<0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the Luminex assay.

claim: No difference was found for the control protein tetanus toxoid (0.8-fold, p=0.85).
source: No such difference was found for the control protein tetanus toxoid (0.8-fold, p=0.85) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the Luminex assay shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Depletion of convalescent COVID-19 sera resulted in a 92% reduction of antibody levels against the SARS-CoV-2 S protein.
source: Depletion of convalescent COVID-19 sera resulted in a 92% reduction of antibody levels against the SARS-CoV-2 S protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the depletion assay.

claim: The reduction of antibodies binding to other hCoV S proteins was strongest for SARS-CoV (61% mean reduction) and MERS-CoV (25%).
source: The reduction of antibodies binding to the other hCoV S proteins was strongest for SARS-CoV (61% mean reduction) and MERS-CoV (25%).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the depletion assay.

claim: A more modest reduction of signal was observed for hCoV-OC43 (13% mean reduction) and hCoV-229E S protein (6%).
source: A more modest reduction of signal was observed for hCoV-OC43 (13% mean reduction) and hCoV-229E S protein (6%), and we observed no depletion of antibodies binding to hCoV-HKU1 (2%) and hCoV-NL63 (–2%).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the depletion assay.

claim: No depletion of antibodies binding to hCoV-HKU1 (2%) and hCoV-NL63 (–2%) was observed.
source: A more modest reduction of signal was observed for hCoV-OC43 (13% mean reduction) and hCoV-229E S protein (6%), and we observed no depletion of antibodies binding to hCoV-HKU1 (2%) and hCoV-NL63 (–2%).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the depletion assay.

claim: Some patients showed up to 72, 70, and 34% reduction of antibodies binding to hCoV-OC43, hCoV-229E and hCoV-HKU1 S protein after depletion, respectively.
source: On the individual level, some patients showed up to 72, 70, and 34% reduction of antibodies binding to hCoV-OC43, hCoV-229E and hCoV-HKU1 S protein after depletion, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the depletion assay.

claim: No reduction in signal was observed for the control protein tetanus toxoid after SARS-CoV-2 S depletion.
source: No reduction in signal was observed for the control protein tetanus toxoid after SARS-CoV-2 S depletion (Figure 2b, Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the depletion assay shown in Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Antibodies binding to other hCoV S proteins in pre-pandemic healthy donor sera did not decrease after depletion.
source: Antibodies binding to other hCoV S proteins in pre-pandemic healthy donor sera did not decrease after depletion (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the depletion assay shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c.

claim: The level of cross-reactivity expressed as the reduction of binding antibodies after depletion by SARS-CoV-2 S protein was associated with the level of sequence identity (Spearman's r = 0.83, p=0.06).
source: Indeed, the level of cross-reactivity expressed as the reduction of binding antibodies after depletion by SARS-CoV-2 S protein was associated with the level of sequence identity (Spearman's r = 0.83, p=0.06) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is a moderate correlation between SARS-CoV-2 neutralization and antibodies binding to SARS-CoV S protein (r = 0.545, p<0.0001).
source: In addition to the observed correlation between SARS-CoV-2 S protein antibody levels and SARS-CoV-2 neutralization, we found a moderate correlation between SARS-CoV-2 neutralization and antibodies binding to SARS-CoV S protein (r = 0.545, p<0.0001), a weak correlation with antibodies that bind to MERS-CoV, hCoV-HKU1, and hCoV-229E S protein (r = 0.324, 0.308, 0.320, respectively, all p<0.05), and no correlation with antibodies binding to hCoV-OC43 and hCoV-NL63 S protein (r = 0.188 and –0.095, p>0.05) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: There is a weak correlation between SARS-CoV-2 neutralization and antibodies that bind to MERS-CoV, hCoV-HKU1, and hCoV-229E S protein (r = 0.324, 0.308, 0.320, respectively, all p<0.05).
source: In addition to the observed correlation between SARS-CoV-2 S protein antibody levels and SARS-CoV-2 neutralization, we found a moderate correlation between SARS-CoV-2 neutralization and antibodies binding to SARS-CoV S protein (r = 0.545, p<0.0001), a weak correlation with antibodies that bind to MERS-CoV, hCoV-HKU1, and hCoV-229E S protein (r = 0.324, 0.308, 0.320, respectively, all p<0.05), and no correlation with antibodies binding to hCoV-OC43 and hCoV-NL63 S protein (r = 0.188 and –0.095, p>0.05) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: There is no correlation between SARS-CoV-2 neutralization and antibodies binding to hCoV-OC43 and hCoV-NL63 S protein (r = 0.188 and –0.095, p>0.05).
source: In addition to the observed correlation between SARS-CoV-2 S protein antibody levels and SARS-CoV-2 neutralization, we found a moderate correlation between SARS-CoV-2 neutralization and antibodies binding to SARS-CoV S protein (r = 0.545, p<0.0001), a weak correlation with antibodies that bind to MERS-CoV, hCoV-HKU1, and hCoV-229E S protein (r = 0.324, 0.308, 0.320, respectively, all p<0.05), and no correlation with antibodies binding to hCoV-OC43 and hCoV-NL63 S protein (r = 0.188 and –0.095, p>0.05) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Cross-reactive antibodies form a minor component of the neutralizing antibodies induced by SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: These correlations suggest that cross-reactive antibodies form a minor component of the neutralizing antibodies induced by SARS-CoV-2 infection.
evidence: This is inferred from the weak or absent correlations between cross-reactive antibodies and neutralization capacity.

claim: After depletion with the SARS-CoV-2 S2 subdomain, a 48, 20, and 19% mean reduction of signal was observed for antibodies binding to SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV, and hCoV-OC43 S protein, respectively.
source: After depletion with the SARS-CoV-2 S2 subdomain, a 48, 20, and 19% mean reduction of signal was observed for antibodies binding to SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV, and hCoV-OC43 S protein, respectively, while no reduction was observed after S1 depletion (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the S1 and S2 subdomain depletion assay shown in Figure 3.

claim: No reduction was observed after S1 depletion.
source: After depletion with the SARS-CoV-2 S2 subdomain, a 48, 20, and 19% mean reduction of signal was observed for antibodies binding to SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV, and hCoV-OC43 S protein, respectively, while no reduction was observed after S1 depletion (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the S1 and S2 subdomain depletion assay shown in Figure 3.

claim: For some individuals, depletion rates reached up to 83% for SARS-CoV, 75% for MERS-CoV, and 80% for hCoV-OC43 S protein after S2 subdomain depletion.
source: For some individuals, depletion rates reached up to 83% for SARS-CoV, 75% for MERS-CoV, and 80% for hCoV-OC43 S protein while there were no individuals with substantial reduction of cross-reactive antibodies after S1 depletion.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the S1 and S2 subdomain depletion assay.

claim: There were no individuals with substantial reduction of cross-reactive antibodies after S1 depletion.
source: For some individuals, depletion rates reached up to 83% for SARS-CoV, 75% for MERS-CoV, and 80% for hCoV-OC43 S protein while there were no individuals with substantial reduction of cross-reactive antibodies after S1 depletion.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the S1 and S2 subdomain depletion assay.

claim: In some individuals the signal was reduced by up to 59% for hCoV-HKU1 and 71% for hCoV-229E S protein following depletion with the SARS-CoV-2 S2 subdomain.
source: However, in some individuals the signal was reduced by up to 59% for hCoV-HKU1 and 71% for hCoV-229E S protein following depletion with the SARS-CoV-2 S2 subdomain, while such effects were not observed after S1 subdomain depletion.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the S1 and S2 subdomain depletion assay.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 S2 subdomain depletion was significantly correlated with S2 sequence identity (r = 0.90, p=0.03).
source: SARS-CoV-2 S2 subdomain depletion was significantly correlated with S2 sequence identity (r = 0.90, p=0.03) while there was no correlation for SARS-CoV-2 S1 subdomain depletion (r = 0.23, p=0.67) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: There was no correlation for SARS-CoV-2 S1 subdomain depletion (r = 0.23, p=0.67).
source: SARS-CoV-2 S2 subdomain depletion was significantly correlated with S2 sequence identity (r = 0.90, p=0.03) while there was no correlation for SARS-CoV-2 S1 subdomain depletion (r = 0.23, p=0.67) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: S2-specific antibodies have a greater contribution to cross-reactivity than S1-specific antibodies.
source: These results indicate that S2-specific antibodies have a greater contribution to cross-reactivity than S1-specific antibodies, which is in accordance with the higher conservation of the S2 subdomain compared to the S1 subdomain (Supplementary file 2; Nguyen-Contant et al., 2020).
evidence: This is inferred from the depletion experiments showing greater reduction with S2 subdomain depletion, and supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The S2 subdomain is more conserved compared to the S1 subdomain.
source: These results indicate that S2-specific antibodies have a greater contribution to cross-reactivity than S1-specific antibodies, which is in accordance with the higher conservation of the S2 subdomain compared to the S1 subdomain (Supplementary file 2; Nguyen-Contant et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature and data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: All macaques developed a detectable increase of antibodies that bind to all hCoV S proteins after vaccination.
source: We observed that all macaques developed a detectable increase of antibodies that bind to all hCoV S proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from vaccinated cynomolgus macaques.

claim: Antibodies binding to SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV, and hCoV-OC43 S proteins were increased compared to baseline by 3313-, 168-, and 106-fold, respectively, in vaccinated macaques.
source: Antibodies binding to SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV, and hCoV-OC43 S proteins were increased compared to baseline by 3313-, 168-, and 106-fold, respectively (Figure 4a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from vaccinated cynomolgus macaques shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Cross-reactivity was already detectable 2 weeks after the first immunization in macaques.
source: This cross-reactivity was already detectable 2 weeks after the first immunization (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from vaccinated cynomolgus macaques shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The induction of antibodies that bind to hCoV-HKU1 and hCoV-229E S proteins was relatively low with a 39- and 16-fold increase from baseline, respectively, in vaccinated macaques.
source: The induction of antibodies that bind to hCoV-HKU1 and hCoV-229E S proteins was relatively low with a 39- and 16-fold increase from baseline, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from vaccinated cynomolgus macaques.

claim: Antibodies binding to hCoV-NL63 S protein showed only a sixfold increase from baseline in vaccinated macaques.
source: Antibodies binding to hCoV-NL63 S protein showed only a sixfold increase from baseline (Figure 4a), and there was no increase observed for tetanus toxoid (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b and c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from vaccinated cynomolgus macaques shown in Figure 4a.

claim: There was no increase observed for tetanus toxoid in vaccinated macaques.
source: Antibodies binding to hCoV-NL63 S protein showed only a sixfold increase from baseline (Figure 4a), and there was no increase observed for tetanus toxoid (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b and c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from vaccinated cynomolgus macaques shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b and c.

claim: Using the SARS-CoV-2 S protein depletion assay, an 88, 98, and 99% mean reduction of antibodies binding to SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV, and hCoV-OC43 S protein, respectively, was observed in vaccinated macaque sera.
source: Using the SARS-CoV-2 S protein depletion assay, an 88, 98, and 99% mean reduction of antibodies binding to SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV, and hCoV-OC43 S protein, respectively, was observed (Figure 4b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the depletion assay on vaccinated macaque sera shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Depletion also resulted in a mean reduction of antibodies binding to proteins hCoV-229E S (92%), hCoV-HKU1 S (92%), and hCoV-NL63 S (75%) in vaccinated macaque sera.
source: In addition, depletion also resulted in a mean reduction of antibodies binding to proteins hCoV-229E S (92%), hCoV-HKU1 S (92%), and hCoV-NL63 S (75%).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the depletion assay on vaccinated macaque sera.

claim: Virtually no depletion (3%) was observed for the control protein tetanus toxoid in vaccinated macaque sera.
source: Virtually no depletion (3%) was observed for the control protein tetanus toxoid (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the depletion assay on vaccinated macaque sera shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The SARS-CoV-2 S protein is capable of inducing cross-reactive antibodies to both alpha and beta hCoVs in macaques.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that the SARS-CoV-2 S protein is capable of inducing cross-reactive antibodies to both alpha and beta hCoVs in macaques.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings in vaccinated macaques.

claim: Antibody levels 3 weeks after the first vaccination and 4 weeks after the second vaccination with the Pfizer-BioNTech mRNA vaccine were compared with baseline results before vaccination in 45 SARS-CoV-2-naïve individuals.
source: Antibody levels 3 weeks after the first vaccination and 4 weeks after the second vaccination with the Pfizer-BioNTech mRNA vaccine were compared with their baseline results before vaccination (Figure 5).
evidence: This describes the experimental design for the human vaccination study.

claim: IgG binding to hCoV S proteins is already increased after the first vaccination in humans.
source: IgG binding to hCoV S proteins is already increased after the first vaccination, but the largest increase in binding was observed following the second vaccination for SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV, and hCoV-OC43 (62-fold, 11-fold, and 2.5-fold, respectively, all p<0.0001) (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from vaccinated humans shown in Figure 5.

claim: The largest increase in binding was observed following the second vaccination for SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV, and hCoV-OC43 (62-fold, 11-fold, and 2.5-fold, respectively, all p<0.0001) in humans.
source: IgG binding to hCoV S proteins is already increased after the first vaccination, but the largest increase in binding was observed following the second vaccination for SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV, and hCoV-OC43 (62-fold, 11-fold, and 2.5-fold, respectively, all p<0.0001) (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from vaccinated humans shown in Figure 5.

claim: The increase observed against hCoV-HKU1 (2.0-fold), hCoV-229E (2.1-fold), and hCoV-NL63 (1.9-fold) was similar to the increase observed for the control protein tetanus toxoid (1.7-fold, p<0.0001) in vaccinated humans.
source: The increase observed against hCoV-HKU1 (2.0-fold), hCoV-229E (2.1-fold), and hCoV-NL63 (1.9-fold) was similar to the increase observed for the control protein tetanus toxoid (1.7-fold, p<0.0001) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from vaccinated humans shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Most cross-reactivity following SARS-CoV-2 vaccination is observed for the most closely related hCoVs.
source: These results confirm our previous findings that most cross-reactivity following SARS-CoV-2 vaccination is observed for the most closely related hCoVs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings in vaccinated humans.

claim: Neutralizing antibodies induced by COVID-19 vaccines have substantially reduced activity against some SARS-CoV-2 variants.
source: A number of studies have shown that neutralizing antibodies induced by COVID-19 vaccines have substantially reduced activity against some SARS-CoV-2 variants (Voysey et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2021; Xie et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Convalescent COVID-19 sera have higher levels of antibodies that bind to other hCoV S proteins compared to pre-pandemic healthy donors.
source: In this study, we show that convalescent COVID-19 sera have higher levels of antibodies that bind to other hCoV S proteins compared to pre-pandemic healthy donors.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding supported by experimental data.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 S protein could partially deplete antibodies binding to all hCoV S proteins except hCoV-NL63 in COVID-19 patient sera.
source: We confirmed this cross-reactivity by showing that SARS-CoV-2 S protein could partially deplete antibodies binding to all hCoV S proteins except hCoV-NL63 in COVID-19 patient sera, while no effect of SARS-CoV-2 S protein depletion was observed in healthy donor sera.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the depletion assay.

claim: No effect of SARS-CoV-2 S protein depletion was observed in healthy donor sera.
